notes.claim: Work is force times the distance moved in the direction of the force, and one joule is the work done when one newton moves something one metre, so work is also newton-metres.
A moment is measured in newton metres, force times perpendicular distance, the same unit product as work but a different quantity.
Power converts to watts only with speed in radians per second, so a speed in rpm must be converted first.
Forces on one object balance when their sum is zero; with no net force an object stays at rest or keeps a constant velocity.
In a two-leg sling each leg tension has a vertical part that carries the load; the two vertical parts together must equal the weight, so each leg pulls harder than half the weight.
The load in each sling leg increases as the angle between the legs increases, and low angles are called extremely hazardous.
The extra tension appears without any extra load being lifted, and the sling itself is no weaker: only the force in each leg grows.
Load angle factors show the rise: leg tension times 1.000 at 90 degrees, 1.155 at 60, 1.414 at 45 and 2.000 at 30, with the angle measured from horizontal (some calculators use vertical).
Static friction matches the push up to a limit, F = μN; once the object slides, kinetic friction is a little smaller, so it is easier to keep it moving than to start it. For lesson i1's crate.
Lubrication makes both the static and the kinetic coefficient of friction considerably smaller. For lesson i1's crate.
A moment is the turning effect of a force about a pivot, and its size is force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
For a body to be balanced the clockwise moments must equal the anticlockwise moments about the pivot.
The moments balance about any point, so one can pick a support as the pivot; that support's own force then has no moment and drops out.
Strain is a fractional change in length, so it has no units, and stress is force per area.
At low stress the deformation is in direct proportion to the stress, and the constant of proportionality is the elastic modulus (Young's modulus for tension), which is the stiffness.
Yield strength marks where plastic (permanent) deformation begins, and the 0.2% offset line is the usual practical way to find it for metals.
Tensile strength is the highest point on the stress-strain curve, a different number from the yield strength and from the modulus.
A shear load acts along the face of a cut, sliding one side past the other, as across a pin or a key; its shear stress is that force over the area of the cut (i3).
A ductile metal stretches a long way and necks before it breaks and soaks up more energy, so it is tougher; a brittle material breaks with hardly any permanent stretch (i3).
Toughness is the energy a material absorbs before it breaks, given by the area under its stress-strain curve (i3).
Hardness is how well a material resists denting or scratching, a different property from stiffness and strength (i3).
A body keeps its motion at constant velocity unless a net external force acts, so constant velocity means zero net force, not a force pushing it along.
Acceleration is proportional to the net external force in the same direction and, as the full law states, inversely proportional to mass, so a net force changes velocity.
Work is force times the distance moved in the direction of the force, and it measures the energy transferred.
Power is work done per unit of time, so the same work done more slowly takes less power.
One joule is the work of one newton moving through one metre.
Rotational power is torque times angular velocity, and the speed must be in radians per second for the result in watts.
A flywheel with a higher moment of inertia, meaning more mass or mass further from the centre, stores more energy at the same speed.
Rotational power is torque times angular velocity, with the speed in radians per second.
A flywheel evens out the speed variations an engine's fluctuating torque would cause, as on a diesel generator (added for i6 at review).
For a gear train the gear ratio is the input speed divided by the output speed; for two gears it matches the teeth or radius ratio.
A belt that does not slip moves at the same speed as the edge of both pulleys.
When a gearbox reduces speed it raises torque in proportion, and a real gearbox loses some power to friction so output power is smaller than input.
Marine diesel engines commonly use a reduction gearbox so the propeller shaft turns slower than the engine.
Shaft misalignment causes vibration, noise and premature bearing, coupling or shaft failure.
Shaft misalignment has no measurable effect on motor efficiency; its harm is vibration, heat and wear (for i7).
Natural frequency is the frequency at which a system would oscillate with no driving or damping, and resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals it.
Away from resonance, as the driving frequency rises above the natural frequency the response gets smaller.
Natural frequency can be changed through stiffness or mass: lower stiffness lowers it.
The rotor speed at which a rotating machine resonates is its critical speed, and machines are designed to run at speeds away from it.
Unbalance force grows with the square of rotating speed, and an unbalance can form a couple that rocks the axis and vibrates the rotor in its bearings.
One guideline for torsional critical speeds is to keep operating speed at least 10 percent clear of them where feasible.
A rigid rotor can be balanced at two end planes, while a flexible rotor needs balancing in several planes.
Misalignment is another source of machine vibration, noise and early bearing or shaft failure.
Vibration monitoring reveals misalignment, unbalance, looseness, worn rolling-element bearings and gear wear.
After unbalance, misalignment is the most common cause of vibration problems in rotating machinery.
Frequency spectrum analysis of vibration tells bearing wear, shaft misalignment and electrically caused vibration apart.
ISO 20816-1 sets general conditions and procedures for measuring and evaluating machine vibration.
